title: Kamma in the moment
hook: the "impulsion" moments where intention does its work

segments.voice: Yesterday, how fast: one moment of matter lasting while seventeen moments of mind arise and pass. Your line: faster than a blink. Did a hard feeling change on the other side of a blink? Day one thousand eighty-five.

A man is asleep under a mango tree with his head covered. A ripe mango drops and brushes past his ear. He wakes, uncovers his head, and looks. He reaches out and picks the fruit up. He squeezes it, sniffs it, decides it's good. Then he eats it. That's a simile the commentaries tell, and every step in it stands for one stage of a single act of perception. The falling fruit, the turning, the looking, the testing. But only one step in the story is the eating. Today, the eating.
screen: `ASLEEP UNDER A MANGO TREE.` → `LOOK, PICK IT UP, TEST IT.` → `THEN HE EATS.`

segments.voice: In the Abhidhamma, when something strikes a sense door, the mind runs through a set series of moments. It turns toward the object. It sees, or hears. It receives, investigates and settles what the thing is. Up to there, none of it is kamma. It's just the mind doing its job, the way the man in the simile wakes, looks and tests. Then come the moments the manual calls javana, a word usually translated impulsion, or running. In an ordinary sense process, the manual says, they usually run seven times in a row. This is the eating. This is where the mind doesn't only know the mango but takes it, likes it, wants it, pushes it away, or meets it with kindness. And this is where the manual locates kamma. In one discourse the Buddha says plainly that intention is what he calls kamma: having intended, a person acts by body, speech and mind. The Abhidhamma takes that sentence and finds its address. Kamma isn't stored in some far-off ledger. It's made in these few running moments, wholesome or unwholesome, again and again, all day. That has a practical side. If kamma is made in javana, then javana is where a life changes direction. You can't stop the mango from falling. You can't unsee it. But the moments that come after seeing are where the taking happens. A pause, a breath, a moment of knowing what you're about to do, and the next run of javana can go a different way. This week the path has run from a soft and workable mind, through restraint and compassion as moments, to matter, a living body, and the speed of it all. Today it lands on the place where all that speed turns into a choice.
screen: `TURN, SEE, RECEIVE, SETTLE.` · `THEN JAVANA RUNS.` · `INTENTION IS KAMMA.` · then, large: `THE PAUSE BEFORE THE TAKING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: pause before one impulse. Sit still and let the body settle. Sooner or later an impulse will come: to scratch an itch, shift your weight, open your eyes, check the time. When it comes, don't follow it right away. Notice it. Name it quietly, wanting to move. Feel what happens during the pause. Then, if you choose to, move, knowing that you're moving. If another impulse arrives, do the same. The bell holds the time.
Javana. Impulsion, the running moments after the mind knows its object, where intention does its work and kamma is made. Today's word.
Your line: where kamma is made. Today, before one reply you're about to send, pause for a single breath, and let the next run of moments choose. Day one thousand eighty-five.

howItsDone: In Theravada Abhidhamma study, students learn the series of mind-moments in a sense process, often through the commentaries' mango simile, and teachers point to the javana moments as the place where kamma is made.

having intended, a person acts by body, speech and mind.

fork.setup: you're the man under the mango tree. the fruit has fallen, you've looked at it and tested it. in the simile, which step stands for javana?
fork.reveal: the eating. the waking, looking and testing stand for the stages before; the eating is javana, the moments that take the object.

original.note: Pali: impulsion, running; the moments in a sense process where intention does its work.

trapdoor: what you thought: kamma is a cosmic score kept somewhere else.
what it means: in the Abhidhamma, kamma is made in a few running moments of mind, right after you know what you're facing.
what a scholar hears: javana, usually seven moments in an ordinary sense process, the manual's address for the sutta line that intention is kamma.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 6.63 (Nibbedhika Sutta), intention is kamma

notes: Week close (days 1079–1085): the teach ends with a one-line look back at the week; confirm it reads naturally.
'Javana usually runs seven times in an ordinary sense process' stated from Abhidhammattha Sangaha IV; confirm.

The mango simile: details vary between tellings (some include the man smelling it, swallowing, then sleeping again). The script tells a simplified version and doesn't map every stage; confirm the source attribution (Atthasalini and the Sangaha commentaries).
'Javana usually translated impulsion, or running': standard renderings; no etymology claimed.
AN 6.63 paraphrased: 'Intention, I tell you, is kamma. Intending, one does kamma by way of body, speech and intellect.' Confirm.
Commentaries hold that the first and seventh javana have special results (in this life / the next); not raised.
